name: Málaga
title: Ship Thickness Measurement in Málaga | UTM for Cruise & Ferries
description: Ultrasonic thickness gauging at Málaga for cruise ships, Melilla ro-pax ferries and bulkers: hull and tank UTM, piping checks and pre-docking steel surveys.
h1: Málaga Ship Gauging: Hull and Tank Thickness Surveys on the Costa del Sol
intro: Málaga is a cruise homeport and ferry gateway on Spain's southern coast, with ro-pax ships sailing to Melilla and a smaller flow of bulk and general cargo. Ships often arrive for a morning and sail by evening, so gauging has to be planned around a published call. We send ultrasonic thickness technicians from India to the vessel, arranged through the ship's agent, and fit the scope to the berth: voids, ballast tanks, car decks, sea-water and scrubber piping, or a sample ahead of an annual survey.

highlights.p: A cruise ship in Málaga has a few hours between disembarkation and sailing. Short, targeted readings in voids, sea-water lines and tanks are agreed with the technical department in advance, so the work stops when the gangway reopens.

highlights.h: Melilla ferry steel and car-deck checks
highlights.p: Ro-pax ships on the Melilla run work hard on ramps, car decks and ballast spaces. Readings taken between rotations give the superintendent measured wastage before the next yard period, rather than estimates from the last survey.

Málaga is rarely where a deep-sea ship is docked. Gauging here helps the owner decide whether to dock in the Bay of Cádiz, at Gibraltar or elsewhere, and what steel to expect the yard to renew, before a slot is committed.

port.h: The port of Málaga: cruise berths, ferries and a working bulk quay
p: The Autoridad Portuaria de Málaga runs a harbour tucked below the city centre, sheltered by long breakwaters and entered from the open Alborán Sea. The approach is straightforward, with the western arm protecting the main basin and the pilots boarding outside the entrance. Because the port sits next to the old town, the passenger berths are only a short walk from the historic centre, and the commercial quays are located further round the basin, separated from the cruise area by fencing and by distance.

Cruise traffic dominates the calendar. Málaga is both a turnaround port, where passengers join and leave, and a port of call, so large ships often berth side by side with the crew working through supply deliveries from early morning. Ferries operate a regular service to Melilla, carrying vehicles, freight trailers and passengers, and the same ships lie alongside between rotations. The cargo side is modest: bulk cargoes, some containers and general cargo arrive through the commercial quays, and a number of tugs, pilot craft and fishing boats share the basin. Visits from naval and research ships appear now and then.

The seasons shape the work. Cruise calls peak from spring to autumn and thin out in winter, which is when ships can make longer stops and when owners schedule dockings elsewhere. Westerly and easterly winds both matter for berthing, and strong levante or poniente conditions can delay a ship or change which quay it is allocated. Anchorage in the bay is used by ships waiting for a berth or for orders, and the tide range is small, so draught and berth depth seldom limit the work. What limits the work is the time alongside, which is why plans are made with the agent before the ship arrives.

Nearly all of the thickness work in Málaga is done alongside. Passenger ships offer the most structured access, because the technical department can have tanks opened, ventilated and tested before arrival, and the ship's own entry procedure covers the team. Ferries on the Melilla route are accessible between rotations, with car decks and ramps easy to reach once the vehicles have gone. Cargo ships at the commercial quays allow hold, hatch coaming and deck work during or after discharge, if the terminal accepts it.

There is no large drydock in the harbour for deep-sea tonnage, so ships needing steel renewal usually dock in the Bay of Cádiz, at Gibraltar or in a larger Mediterranean yard. The port has facilities for smaller craft such as tugs, workboats and fishing boats, and these can be hauled out or worked afloat by local repair firms. For anything larger, the useful job in Málaga is to establish the wastage picture, so the docking yard is chosen and briefed on measured data. Ships waiting in the bay can be gauged at anchor only for short jobs, subject to launch access and weather.
list: Cruise terminals on the passenger quays — voids, ballast and service tanks, sea-water cooling lines and scrubber piping on turnaround days
Ferry berths for Melilla services — car decks, ramps, hoistable decks and ballast tanks between rotations
Commercial quays — hold, hatch coaming, deck and tank readings on bulk and general cargo ships during or after discharge
Repair quay used by tugs and workboats — hull plating readings on harbour craft before a haul-out elsewhere
Málaga Bay anchorage — a short sampling job for a ship waiting for orders, subject to weather and launch access

context.h: Regulation, port state control and trade around Málaga
p: Ships calling at Málaga are subject to port state control under the Paris MoU, carried out in Spain by the Capitanías Marítimas under the Dirección General de la Marina Mercante. Inspectors are particularly interested in structural condition and in the fire main, bilge and ballast piping when ships have carried out long periods without a docking. Measured readings from a recent gauging help a master explain wastage to an inspector and show that steel has been assessed rather than ignored. Passenger ships and ro-pax ferries also face attention to the integrity of watertight bulkheads and doors.

EU rules add pressure for owners with a long-term plan. The Ship Recycling Regulation requires ships calling at EU ports to carry an up-to-date Inventory of Hazardous Materials, EU ETS covers emissions from ships on EU voyages, and FuelEU Maritime now applies to energy use. Cruise lines and ferry operators in this corner of Spain are investing in shore power and cleaner fuel, and any retrofit that opens up structure is a good moment to take a baseline set of thickness readings. Where tonnage is old, the data also informs decisions on whether to renew steel, sell or lay up.

jobs.h: Typical thickness gauging jobs in Málaga
jobs.p: The jobs seen at Málaga follow the calls: short work on cruise ships and ferries, and longer, more thorough surveys on cargo ships that spend more time alongside. Scope, access and report layout are settled with the superintendent in advance, so that the berth hours go on readings instead of orientation. Examples of the work that suits this port:
list: Cruise ship void and sea-water line gauging on a turnaround day, with the technical department opening spaces ahead of the team's arrival.
Melilla ferry car-deck, ramp and ballast tank readings taken across several rotations ahead of an annual survey.
Pre-docking sampling of ballast tanks and deck plating on a bulk carrier, giving the owner a steel estimate before booking a yard.
Scrubber overboard pipe and hull penetration gauging on a passenger ship, compared with readings taken at the previous visit.
Owner's condition gauging on a ship offered for sale or entering a new charter in the Alborán Sea.

logistics: Málaga-Costa del Sol Airport has regular connections with European and Gulf hubs, which suits technicians travelling from India, and the port is a short road trip from the terminal. The ship's agent arranges port passes, gangway access and a launch if the ship is at anchor. Schengen visas are needed for the team, so please send the vessel's dates early; for a planned ferry or cruise programme that is easy, and for a short-notice call we confirm what is possible once visas are issued.

faqs.q: Can a cruise ship be gauged during a Málaga turnaround?
faqs.a: Yes, within limits. A turnaround day allows readings in voids, sea-water lines and tanks that the technical department has prepared, provided entry permits and gas-free certificates are in place before the team boards. Larger programmes involving staging or full tank cleaning are better left to a dry-dock period, which cruise ships usually take outside the Costa del Sol season.

faqs.q: Is there a drydock in Málaga for renewal work?
faqs.a: Not for deep-sea ships. Harbour craft and small vessels are handled by local repair firms, but cargo ships and passenger ships needing steel renewal normally dock in the Bay of Cádiz, at Gibraltar or elsewhere in the Mediterranean. Thickness gauging in Málaga helps you choose the yard and brief it with measured data, so the docking scope is not a surprise.

faqs.q: Can the team work on a ferry between Melilla rotations?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Car decks, ramps, ballast tanks and piping can be gauged across several lay-overs when the crew prepares access in advance. Work that needs gas-freeing of fuel tanks or heavy staging fits better into an overhaul period, when the ship is out of service anyway and the programme can be completed in one sitting.

faqs.q: What if the ship is anchored in the bay?
faqs.a: Short jobs are possible, but they depend on launch availability, swell and the agent's clearance. Most ships at anchor are waiting for a berth and may move at short notice, so a targeted list of spaces works better than a broad programme. If the stay is likely to be long, a berth is a safer place to carry out the survey.

faqs.q: Do you provide thickness reports in the class formats?
faqs.a: We issue readings in a layout that follows the common class thickness measurement report formats, so the surveyor and superintendent can read them easily. Whether a report is accepted for credit to a particular survey is decided by the classification society and the surveyor, and that is explained in the class section further down this page.
